headline: Prefer shorter-dated Australian credit over long-duration government bonds and offshore debt; local market offers better relative value after hedging costs
reasoning: Tyler's preferred approach to insulating a portfolio is to hold shorter-dated credit, which can deliver similar income to longer-duration government bonds without the associated volatility. He favours Australian local debt over offshore alternatives because hedging costs erode the yield pickup on offshore paper. He notes that the Australian market is now a strong hunting ground, a marked contrast to the sub-100bp yield environment Daintree navigated during COVID, and welcomes the current high-yield world for income-oriented investors.
quote: For us our portfolio is very much about shorter dated credit. We can get similar amounts of income without all the volatility that comes from from higher government bond yields. And we think for now that's a more sensible way of building portfolios. And whereabouts where you're looking. Um, local debt is is better relative value than offshore. Because as soon as you start hedging offshore debt, you give away some of the yield pickup that you might otherwise receive.
episode_title: How to insulate your portfolio from the global bond sell-off

headline: Rising yields driven by multiple forces: central bank policy repricing, excess demand for capital from hyperscalers, and sovereign fiscal stress — with US 10-year at a 24-year high
reasoning: Tyler identifies a confluence of drivers pushing yields higher globally. Markets continue to reprice the terminal policy rate upward across multiple countries, causing underperformance along the entire yield curve. Inflation-linked bonds are not outperforming nominals, suggesting the market believes central banks will do their job and keep tightening. Additionally, massive capital demand from AI hyperscalers and other borrowers is competing for available savings, reversing the pre-COVID excess-savings regime. The combination of inflation and seemingly profligate government spending is prompting the bond market to push back on sovereign creditworthiness, particularly in France which lacks the option of unconventional monetary policy.
quote: You would expect the market to take fear from that. And you'd expect the inflationary bonds would do better than nominal bonds in this environment. We're not actually seeing that right. So what it says to you is that, sure we're in an inflationary environment, but central banks are going to do their job right. They're going to push um, yields up. And so you are seeing, Underperformance all the way along the yield curve, because people just keep reassessing what the final policy rate is going to be in a whole range of different markets. So that's part of it. Um, that is causing sovereign stress in particular in France, because unlike in other countries, France can't print money to to, you know, sort of that's not one of the options available to it.

headline: Structural shift to higher inflation driven by deglobalisation, supply chain resilience costs and tariffs is turning traditional portfolio relationships on their head
reasoning: Justin Tyler argues the world has undergone a structural change toward higher inflation, not merely a cyclical shift. Post-COVID, governments, corporates and individuals all desire resilience in supply chains, moving away from just-in-time models, which costs money and drives inflation. Tariffs and trade restrictions add further upward pressure. The disinflationary tailwinds of globalisation have run their course, meaning the usual inverse relationship between bonds and equities no longer reliably holds.
quote: I would say is that a lot of, um, of the debate is because people always like to debate cyclical changes, right? But actually, I think that we're seeing a structural change. We're seeing a structural change whereby the world is more inflationary than what it used to be. Um, and that turns the usual sort of portfolio relationships on, on their head.
episode_title: How to insulate your portfolio from the global bond sell-off

headline: France is a key sovereign risk to watch — lacks monetary sovereignty to inflate away debt unlike the US, making it more vulnerable to bond market pressure
reasoning: Tyler singles out France as the sovereign most at risk from the current bond selloff, because unlike the US, France cannot resort to unconventional monetary policy or currency debasement to manage its debt burden. The US retains the advantage of reserve currency status and has historical precedent (post-WWII) for using unconventional policy. Tyler frames unexpected inflation as a historical mechanism by which heavily indebted sovereigns effectively default in real terms, and warns that the bond market will increasingly resist profligate fiscal behaviour when combined with an inflationary backdrop.
quote: That is causing sovereign stress in particular in France, because unlike in other countries, France can't print money to to, you know, sort of that's not one of the options available to it. Whereas in the US, you might argue that unconventional monetary policy is on the table, as we saw post World War two... when you have big sovereign debt loads, one way that sovereigns work their way through that, which is another way of saying default on part of that is that you have unexpected inflation, because it means that that debt in today's dollars is worth less than it was yesterday. So as soon as you have that combination of inflation and, you know, uh, just wildly almost, I'd say profligate, you know, government spending, the bond market does say, yeah, yeah, yeah... I think we need to keep our eyes on France.

headline: AI hyperscaler capex is a persistent source of capital demand pressuring yields; market yet to question whether all this spending will be productive
reasoning: Tyler notes that the enormous capital spending by AI hyperscalers is a significant and likely sustained driver of global capital demand, which puts upward pressure on bond yields. He observes the same dynamic playing out in Australia with large capital market issuance. While history suggests a portion of this capital spending will not prove productive, the market is currently focused solely on which model builders will achieve a dominant position and is not yet pricing in any capital-efficiency concerns. He does not expect this capex wave to abate in the near term.
quote: Absolutely it is. You know, and we saw that a couple of weeks ago in Australia. You know, there was a big issue here, but more, you know, globally you are seeing a lot of demand for capital, as I said, and a lot of it's coming from, from these hyperscalers. Um, I don't think that that's necessarily going to stop anytime soon. You know, at the end of the day, the market would need to reassess whether this capital spending is actually going to all be productive capital spending. I think history would say that that there will be a portion of it that won't be. But at the moment the market's not interested in that. It's all about, you know, which of these model builders is is going to end up in the preeminent position.

headline: No catalyst for bond yields to rally strongly; asymmetric upside argument requires a credible trigger that is absent
reasoning: Tyler acknowledges the mathematical argument that bonds are now asymmetric — that coupon flows limit downside while a large yield rally would produce an outsized payoff — but he challenges this by demanding a clear catalyst for that rally. In the current structural environment of persistent inflation and deglobalisation, he sees no convincing reason for yields to fall materially, making the asymmetry argument less compelling in practice.
quote: I'd say, yeah, that's true. As long as you can give me a catalyst as to why yields are going to rally that that much. And I think that's the key with the changes that I've talked about. I can't see a reason for for bond yields to to rally strongly from here.
episode_title: How to insulate your portfolio from the global bond sell-off

headline: Structural shift to positive bond-equity correlation makes long-duration bonds obsolete as portfolio defence; 60/40 framework is dead in an inflationary world
reasoning: Tyler argues that the historically negative correlation between bonds and equities has structurally flipped positive, driven by a persistently inflationary global environment. Historical precedent shows that when inflation is neither low nor stable, bonds and equities tend to move together. This means long-tenor bonds no longer reliably cushion portfolios against equity drawdowns, fundamentally undermining the 60/40 allocation framework. The implication is that investors need to rethink portfolio construction entirely rather than treating this as a cyclical phenomenon.
quote: The fact that this correlation between bonds and and equities used to be negative and now it's positive. Um, we think that's actually a structural change in the market. And I discussed this last time I was on um you have an inflationary world now right. And history shows that when inflation is neither low nor stable, then typically you end up with a positive correlation between bonds and equities. And so it really calls into question whether you need long tenor bonds in your portfolio as a defense anymore, right? There's various reasons to have them. But that old sort of way of building a portfolio with 60/40, um, we think that's dead now.
episode_title: How to insulate your portfolio from the global bond sell-off

headline: AI capex spending is a key watch item; any reconsideration of its productivity could trigger an equity turning point
reasoning: While equity markets continue to rise despite competition from high bond yields, Tyler identifies a potential inflection point: if investors begin to question whether massive capital expenditure on AI infrastructure will prove productive, that could cause a meaningful reassessment of equity valuations. He does not see this happening imminently but flags it as the most credible near-term risk to the current equity rally.
quote: If you're going to watch for a turning point here, it's for people reconsidering the capital spending in the AI space and whether all of that's going to be productive if you start to see some weakness there. I can't see that happening anytime soon.
